entities.summary:
Johannes Hültz, a master builder of the Late Gothic period, emerged from Cologne around 1390 to become a pivotal figure in the architectural history of the Holy Roman Empire, most notably for completing the iconic north spire of Strasbourg Cathedral. His work, culminating in 1439, not only established the cathedral as the world's tallest building for over two centuries but also exemplified a distinctive style of openwork tracery that influenced subsequent generations of German Gothic architects. Hültz's contributions stand as a testament to the sophisticated engineering and artistic ambition of 15th-century European craftsmanship, pushing the boundaries of structural possibility.

Hültz's career is inextricably linked to Strasbourg Cathedral, where he likely began working on the spire around 1419, eventually assuming the role of master builder in 1439. He inherited and refined the designs of his predecessors, including Erwin von Steinbach, to realize the spire's final, audacious form. His design featured an intricate octagonal lantern crowned by a delicate, openwork filigree spire, soaring to an unprecedented height of 142 meters (466 feet). This complex construction required precise stonecutting, advanced scaffolding techniques, and a profound understanding of structural mechanics, allowing the massive stone structure to appear remarkably light and ethereal.
